title: Developmental anomalies of the teeth
blurb: Missing and extra teeth, inherited enamel and dentine defects, fluorosis and tetracycline staining: what goes wrong while teeth form, and why.
question: A 9-year-old's upper left central incisor came through two years ago, but the right one still hasn't appeared. A radiograph shows a small, cone-shaped extra tooth between the roots of the central incisors. What is this extra tooth called, and why might it be stopping the incisor erupting?

teach.h: Problems that start before a tooth erupts
teach.body: Teeth develop in stages: the tooth bud forms (deciding how many teeth), takes its shape and size, then lays down and mineralises enamel and dentine, and finally erupts. A problem at each stage gives a different anomaly: the wrong number of teeth, an odd size or shape, faulty structure, or abnormal colour. Causes can be inherited (genetic), general (illness, medicines or too much fluoride while teeth form), or local (infection or injury to a baby tooth). Enamel is laid down only once, so defects formed in childhood last for life.

children.label: Size & shape
children.sub: Peg laterals, fused or bent teeth

teach.body: Hypodontia is the developmental absence of one or more teeth. Third molars are most often missing; after them, upper lateral incisors and lower second premolars. Six or more missing (not counting third molars) is oligodontia; all missing (anodontia) is very rare. Hypodontia is more common with Down syndrome, cleft lip and palate, and ectodermal dysplasia. Supernumerary teeth are extras. The commonest is a mesiodens between the upper central incisors, which can block a central incisor erupting or cause a gap (diastema). Upper lateral incisors may also be small and peg-shaped.

teach.caption: Upper lateral incisors (12, 22) and lower second premolars (35, 45) congenitally absent. A tooth missing from the mouth may simply be unerupted, so the dentist confirms absence with a radiograph.
Both are inherited, so other family members are often affected. Osteogenesis imperfecta is 'brittle bone disease'.

teach.h: Stains built in while the tooth forms
teach.body: These are intrinsic stains: inside the tooth, so they cannot be polished off. Fluorosis is caused by too much fluoride swallowed while enamel is forming in early childhood, for example eating toothpaste or using too much. Mild fluorosis shows as white flecks or lines; severe fluorosis as brown mottling and pitting. Tetracycline antibiotics bind to calcium in developing teeth, leaving grey, brown or yellow bands. That is why tetracyclines are not given to children under 12 or to pregnant or breastfeeding women.

Molar incisor hypomineralisation (MIH) affects one or more first permanent molars, often with the incisors. The enamel has clearly edged creamy, yellow or brown patches, is soft and can break down soon after eruption. Affected teeth can be very sensitive and hard to numb, so children may find treatment difficult. Enamel hypoplasia means enamel that is thin or missing in places. It can follow a serious illness in early childhood, or infection or injury to a baby tooth damaging the permanent tooth forming beneath it (a 'Turner tooth').

teach.text: Don't confuse the two 'imperfectas': AMELOgenesis = ENAMEL (think ameloblasts), DENTINOgenesis = DENTINE. And fluorosis and tetracycline are intrinsic stains: they can't be polished off like tea, coffee or tobacco stains.

items: Hypodontia: teeth absent from birth; after third molars, upper laterals and lower second premolars.
Supernumeraries: extra teeth; a mesiodens between the upper centrals can block eruption.
Amelogenesis imperfecta = inherited enamel defect; dentinogenesis imperfecta = inherited dentine defect.
Fluorosis: too much fluoride while enamel forms; white flecks to brown pitting.
Tetracycline: grey-brown bands; not given under 12 or in pregnancy.

summary: You can now explain how problems at each stage of tooth development cause anomalies of number, shape, structure and colour; recognise hypodontia and supernumerary teeth; tell amelogenesis from dentinogenesis imperfecta; and explain how fluorosis and tetracycline staining arise and how they are prevented.

A.q: What is the term for the developmental absence of one or more teeth?
A.why: Hypodontia means one or more teeth failed to develop.

whyNot.2: Microdontia means teeth that are smaller than normal.
whyNot.3: Dilaceration is a sharp bend in a tooth's root or crown.

A.q: Where is a mesiodens usually found?
options: Palatal to the upper first permanent molars
A.why: A mesiodens is a supernumerary tooth in the midline between the upper central incisors, the commonest site for an extra tooth.

whyNot.0: Teeth behind the third molars are called distomolars, and are rare.
whyNot.1: This is not where a mesiodens develops.
whyNot.3: Extra teeth here are uncommon and are not called a mesiodens.

A.q: Why are tetracycline antibiotics avoided in children under 12?
options: They make the enamel unusually hard
A.why: Tetracyclines bind to calcium in developing teeth and bone, causing permanent grey, brown or yellow banded staining.

whyNot.0: Gum overgrowth is linked to drugs such as phenytoin, ciclosporin and nifedipine.
whyNot.2: Tetracycline stains teeth; it does not harden enamel.
whyNot.3: Delayed eruption is not the reason tetracyclines are avoided.

B.q: A patient has amber, see-through teeth whose enamel chips off easily. She has had several fractured bones since childhood. Which condition is most likely?
B.why: Dentinogenesis imperfecta gives opalescent amber or blue-grey teeth whose enamel flakes off weak dentine, and it is linked with osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bones).

whyNot.0: Amelogenesis imperfecta affects enamel and is not linked with brittle bones.
whyNot.1: Tetracycline causes banded grey-brown staining, not chipping enamel.
whyNot.2: Fluorosis causes white or brown mottling, not opalescent teeth.

B.q: A 7-year-old has white flecks and lines on his new front teeth. His parent says he has always used a large blob of adult toothpaste and likes to eat it. What is the most likely cause?
B.why: Swallowing too much fluoride while enamel forms causes fluorosis, which in mild form shows as white flecks and lines.

whyNot.0: Early caries shows as white spots near the gum or between teeth, linked to plaque and sugar.
whyNot.2: Dentinogenesis imperfecta gives amber or blue-grey teeth.
whyNot.3: Tetracycline gives grey-brown bands, not white flecks.

B.q: After third molars, which teeth are most commonly missing in hypodontia?
B.why: After third molars, upper lateral incisors and lower second premolars are the teeth most often congenitally absent.

whyNot.0: First molars are very rarely missing.
whyNot.1: Lower central incisors are not among the most commonly missing teeth.
whyNot.3: Upper canines are rarely absent, though they are often impacted.

C.q: A patient's mother and brother have the same thin, yellow-brown, easily chipped enamel. Which tissue is defective in amelogenesis imperfecta?
C.why: Amelogenesis imperfecta is an inherited defect in how enamel forms, affecting both dentitions.

whyNot.0: Dentine is affected in dentinogenesis imperfecta.
whyNot.1: Cementum covers the root and is not the tissue affected in AI.
whyNot.2: The pulp is soft tissue and is not the defective tissue in AI.

C.q: Which of these is an intrinsic stain that cannot be removed by polishing?
C.why: Tetracycline is built into the tooth as it forms, so the stain is intrinsic.

whyNot.0: Tea and coffee cause extrinsic stain on the surface, which can be polished off.
whyNot.1: Tobacco stain is extrinsic and can be removed by scaling and polishing.
whyNot.3: Chlorhexidine causes extrinsic brown staining that can be polished off.

C.q: A parent asks how much toothpaste to use for her 2-year-old to protect the teeth without risking fluorosis. What is the best advice?
options: A full brush-length, then rinse well
C.why: Delivering Better Oral Health advises a smear of toothpaste with at least 1,000 ppm fluoride for children under 3, with an adult supervising.

whyNot.1: Too much toothpaste increases swallowed fluoride, and rinsing washes away the benefit.
whyNot.2: Brushing with fluoride toothpaste should start as soon as the first tooth appears.
whyNot.3: Fluoride-free paste gives no protection against caries; the answer is the right amount, not no fluoride.

reteach.title: Building a wall, brick by brick
reteach.question: Imagine building a garden wall. What could go wrong with the number of bricks, their shape, the quality of the mortar, or something mixed into it?

blocks.h: Four places a build can go wrong
blocks.body: The wrong number of bricks delivered: too few is hypodontia, too many is a supernumerary. A faulty brick mould: an odd-shaped tooth, like a peg lateral. Poor-quality material: weak enamel (amelogenesis imperfecta) or weak dentine underneath (dentinogenesis imperfecta). Something mixed into the wet mortar: too much fluoride (fluorosis) or tetracycline (bands of stain). Once the wall has set, you can't change what's inside it, which is why these defects are permanent.

blocks.h: What went wrong, and the result
head: What went wrong
Anomaly

blocks.text: Timing is everything: fluoride and tetracycline only cause these stains while teeth are still forming, which is why the risk is in pregnancy and childhood, not adulthood.

explain.body: A supernumerary is an extra tooth. A mesiodens sits between the upper central incisors and is often cone-shaped. It can stop a central incisor erupting, push teeth out of line or leave a gap. The dentist usually arranges its removal, sometimes with orthodontics.

explain.caption: 11 unerupted while 21 is through: a classic sign that something, often a mesiodens, is in the way.

test.q: An upper central incisor has failed to erupt more than a year after its partner. What may a radiograph reveal?
options: A supernumerary tooth in the way
Severe fluorosis of the incisor enamel
test.why: A mesiodens or other supernumerary tooth is a common reason for a central incisor failing to erupt.

whyNot.1: Fluorosis affects enamel appearance, not eruption.
whyNot.3: DI affects dentine quality, and both incisors would be affected.

explain.body: Amelogenesis imperfecta is an inherited enamel defect: thin, pitted or soft enamel that wears and chips. Dentinogenesis imperfecta is an inherited dentine defect: amber or blue-grey teeth whose enamel flakes off weak dentine, linked with brittle bone disease.

explain.caption: AI affects the outer enamel; DI affects the dentine beneath it.

test.q: Dentinogenesis imperfecta is associated with which general condition?
test.why: Dentinogenesis imperfecta can occur with osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bone disease), as both involve faulty collagen.

whyNot.0: Down syndrome is linked with hypodontia and other dental features, not DI.
whyNot.2: Diabetes affects periodontal health, not dentine formation.
whyNot.3: Cleft lip and palate is linked with missing and extra teeth.

explain.body: Fluorosis comes from swallowing too much fluoride while enamel forms in early childhood. Prevent it with the right amount of toothpaste: a smear under 3, a pea-sized amount from 3 to 6, brushing supervised, spit not rinse. Fluoride toothpaste is still essential; the dose is what matters.

test.q: What amount of toothpaste does Delivering Better Oral Health advise for a child aged 3–6?
test.why: Children aged 3–6 should use a pea-sized amount of toothpaste with at least 1,000 ppm fluoride, spitting not rinsing.

whyNot.0: A smear is for children under 3.
whyNot.2: A full brush-length is far too much and raises fluorosis risk.
whyNot.3: Half a brush-length is still more than advised.

explain.body: Tetracycline taken by a mother in pregnancy, or by a child while the teeth form, binds to calcium in the developing teeth. The result is permanent grey, brown or yellow bands. It cannot be polished off; cosmetic options include bleaching or veneers.

test.q: A 10-year-old has grey-brown horizontal bands across his permanent front teeth. He had several courses of antibiotics as a toddler. Which drug group is most likely responsible?
test.why: Tetracyclines bind to calcium in developing teeth and cause banded intrinsic staining.

whyNot.0: Penicillins do not stain developing teeth.
whyNot.1: Metronidazole does not cause intrinsic tooth staining.
whyNot.3: Macrolides such as erythromycin do not cause banded staining.
